subject: Behavioral Economics
title: The Availability Cascade
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: The Availability Cascade.

hook.text: A rare disease gets media attention. Suddenly everyone thinks it's an epidemic. Nothing changed.

buildup.text: Repeated media coverage makes events feel common. Each story triggers more stories, feeding the loop.

discovery.text: An availability cascade: belief spreads because the idea is repeated, not because it's true.

twist.text: Public fear then drives policy changes for a threat that remains statistically tiny.

climax.text: The volume of a story determines its perceived importance. Frequency of mention beats actual frequency.

quiz.question: What drives an availability cascade?
options: Repeated mention making an idea feel common

details.summary: An availability cascade is a self-reinforcing cycle where a belief gains credibility through repetition in public discourse. As more people discuss a claim, it feels more plausible, generating more discussion, which makes it seem even more credible regardless of its truth.
details.whyItMatters: Availability cascades drive moral panics, stock market bubbles, and policy overreactions to rare risks. Once a narrative achieves critical mass in public discourse, its perceived truth becomes nearly independent of actual evidence.
takeaways: Repeated claims feel truer regardless of their factual basis
Media coverage creates feedback loops that amplify perceived risk
Cascades can drive policy responses disproportionate to actual threats

faq.question: How does an availability cascade start?
faq.answer: A memorable event or claim gets media coverage. People discuss it, making it more available mentally. This discussion generates more coverage. Each cycle makes the claim feel more credible and common, regardless of whether the underlying risk changed.

faq.question: Can availability cascades be stopped?
faq.answer: They are very difficult to stop once started because attempting to debunk the claim generates more discussion, further increasing availability. Effective responses require persistent counter-narratives and de-escalation of media attention.
